PRODSECRM-316.summary: OCP mixed el8/el9 images on a single Konflux advisory CPE (temporary skip of check-labels CPE match)
PRODSECRM-316.description:
Exception Title: OCP mixed el8/el9 images on a single Konflux advisory CPE (temporary skip of check-labels CPE match)
Exception Type: Conforma - Konflux/ EC policy check, blocking release
Business Unit: Hybrid Platforms
Product: Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform
Conforma MR Link: Not Applicable / Not a Conforma Exception
Exception Reason:
Konflux RPAs support one CPE per advisory. OCP z-streams still ship a mixed payload (el8 and el9 images on the same release). Image labels already have the correct per-image CPEs (::el8 vs ::el9).
After release-service-catalog PR #2451 (https://github.com/konflux-ci/release-service-catalog/pull/245, production ~7 Sep 2026), "enforceContainerFirstSecurityLabels" can no longer be turned off. Release check-labels now requires every image CPE to match the RPA CPE, so mixed OCP releases fail.
OCP is not ready to split to multiple payload advisories this week (https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/ART-14748#icft=ART-14748
: single payload advisory ID; Cincinnati, ERT, Release Controller, docs). This exception is time-boxed ProdSec acceptance of continuing the existing Konflux CSAF/VEX pattern (one advisory CPE for mixed OCI images) so blocked z-streams and stage can ship. It is not a Conforma exception and not approval of a global override (PR #2537 - https://github.com/konflux-ci/release-service-catalog/pull/2537). Workaround must stay OCP-scoped (CI/constraint), with name and timestamp checks remaining enforced if the pipeline can split those gates.
Risk of Approving Exception:
Residual risk is incorrect OpenShift product-variant CPE on Konflux container (OCI) entries in CSAF/VEX, not shipping the wrong bits.
- The payload still ships the correct images; image CPEs stay correct.

- The advisory/CSAF can list el8 images as components of an el9 product (or the reverse), depending on the single RPA CPE. This is already in production data, e.g. CVE-2025-65637 VEX (https://security.access.redhat.com/data/csaf/v2/vex/2025/cve-2025-65637.json) for RHSA-2026:6493 (https://access.redhat.com/errata/RHSA-2026:6493): ose-openshift-apiserver-rhel8 (and other *-rhel8 images) related to the Konflux 4.12 product whose CPE is cpe:/a:redhat:openshift:4.12::el9, not 8Base-RHOSE-4.12. The ::el8 CPE in that VEX is on the RPM 8Base-RHOSE-4.12 node, not those OCI images.

- Scanners that match VEX by OpenShift CPE first, then the image can miss the container-level fix (false positives) for the mismatched RHEL slice. Digest-only scanners may still mark the image fixed. RPM/content-set scanning is a separate path and is not this defect.

- If the workaround is implemented as a global override, name-label (VEX identity) and related checks can regress for other products. That is a higher risk and is out of scope of this exception.

This does not waive signing, Conforma “labels must exist,” or timestamp tags, unless Release implements a blunt global disable (which this exception must not authorize).
Impact if Exception NOT Approved:
- Missed OCP z-stream (and stage) this week / next: ART reports most scheduled z-streams blocked; stage blocked for 4.12–4.15; Sustaining needed 4.12, 4.13, 4.18. Those payloads include security fixes.

- Customers do not get those rebuilt images until a split-RPA/multi-advisory design lands - work that ART says is a product/process change (payload metadata is a single advisory field), not a same-week Konflux toggle.

- Engineering would still need https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/ART-14748#icft=ART-14748
 (and stakeholder decisions for Cincinnati/ERT/docs) regardless; refusing the exception does not finish that work this week. It only holds security content behind a metadata check.

Proposed Remediation:
Permanent fix (pick one; both are tracked):
- Preferred near-term product path: https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/ART-14748#icft=ART-14748
 - split RPAs so each RHEL version gets its own advisory/CPE (design already written/reviewed; implementation and the single payload-advisory-ID decision still required). Ticket must leave New with an owner and target date as a condition of this exception.

- Platform alternative (longer): https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/KONFLUX-6854#icft=KONFLUX-6854
 - multiple CPEs on one advisory (Errata Tool–like). Still New / not a this-quarter unblock.

While the exception is open:
- Scoped pipeline/CI constraint so only OCP mixed-stream RPAs skip CPE match; default remains enforce=true; no global RPA boolean for all tenants.

- Keep name and timestamp enforcement on.

- Expiry / review: expire when https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/ART-14748#icft=ART-14748
 or https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/KONFLUX-6854#icft=KONFLUX-6854
 is in production. Re-review before renewal; do not treat this as standing policy.
Approving VP Email: scuppett@redhat.com
Exception Expiration: 10/3/2026
Additional Watchers: asdas@redhat.com, vlaad@redhat.com, ppostler@redhat.com, jdelft@redhat.com
Related Risk Ticket: N/A

comments.author: Joep Delft
comments.body:
We just got hit by this requirement, as https://github.com/konflux-ci/release-service-catalog/pull/2451
  merged. Getting more than one advisory describing the payload is a change that will take some investigations and negotiations with stake holders to implement. Some topics to work out:
how to embed in payload
OCP is embedding “the payload advisory” into the metadata of the payload. This is a single field, and there are some (internal, but maybe also external) users who read this value. We should either opt for breaking this by listing multiple separated by, say, a comma, or choose a single advisory to be “the one”.
Both options might need external communication. 
how to wire this into ART tooling
Splitting “the payload advisory” into multiple will need some adjustments:
- in promote (embed the right metadata)

- in prepare-release (so advisories get split)

- in in the RPAs

- in GitLab CI pipelines

- with documentation text

other teams
Depending on the decision of how to embed what in payload these teams might need to adjust their tooling/processes:
- ERT (for advisory verification)

- Cincinatti: For parsing the advisory info to put the release in fast stream

- Release Controller: Is possibly also inspecting this field

- Docs crew (looks at advisories and may have tooling)

- Product: Might need to document this change

ART-14748.description:
Background
The check-labels task (enforceContainerFirstSecurityLabels) enforces that the CPE label on images matches the RPA's CPE. Each advisory is associated with a single CPE (either el8 or el9).
OCP versions like 4.12 have a mix of images - some are el8 (e.g. kube-rbac-proxy, ovn-kubernetes in 4.12) and some are el9. The RPA currently has a single CPE annotation (e.g. el9), which causes the check to fail for el8 images.
Proposed Solution
Split RPAs for versions with differing rhelness into two RPAs each: one for el8 images, one for el9 images.
This aligns with how prodsec tooling consumes the data - separate RHSAs are needed for el8 vs el9 content when shipping security fixes.
Scope
• Update konflux-release-data: Create separate RPAs per RHEL version for affected OCP versions (e.g. 4.12, 4.15 during RHEL migration)
• Update art-tools automation: Route components to the correct RPA based on their rhelness (many moving parts - builds, shipments, etc.)
Context
Discussed in thread: https://redhat-internal.slack.com/archives/CB95J6R4N/p1768922278919739
Implementation plan
Detailed design and rollout (compound shipment kinds, repo/file touchpoints, automation and per-version rollout order):

https://docs.google.com/document/d/1fKCjDcz9Ef49irjJ3rb35f1Nl85BIAg6a90uoyoWyJQ/edit

comments.author: Przemyslaw Roguski
comments.body:
Using bundled "Dockerfiles" was prone to mistakes because in many cases the "Labels" are maintained by people and are not up to date.
To somehow address this problem ProdSec created https://security.access.redhat.com/data/metrics/container-name-repos-map.json which mapped the incorrect "name" label from the container Dockerfile to the real repository and container name. But even that workaround is not good, because:
- it's complex and it's not well documented

- contains incorrect (not up to date) data

- it's not officially maintained

 
Instead of searching and using bundled Dockerfiles (which are missing even today in the legacy build system many times) it's better to inspect the container image metadata and read the "RepoTags", which is set by the release pipeline.
The public repository name and container image name is what is necessary to find the right Container First Security metadata in the CSAF/VEX files.
Architecture information is additional helper.
 
For example, for built in Konflux registry.redhat.io/rhel9/nginx-124:9.5-1730563934, the metadata "RepoTags:" is following:
"RepoTags": [
               "registry.redhat.io/rhel9/nginx-124:9.5-1730563934"
          ],
          "RepoDigests": [
               "registry.redhat.io/rhel9/nginx-124@sha256:04cf31e9a3874781ab2c0f3b0fa5963ca5beed1aa1a3d36d5896337bedee523f",
               "registry.redhat.io/rhel9/nginx-124@sha256:3a8ca1039acd462bc89a55de791b05ba73b064308aff87c7704ce1f94bbefeb0"
          ],
 
 
 
Using Dockerfile labels many times is incorrect, for example see rhoai/odh-rhel8-operator Dockerfile:
https://catalog.redhat.com/software/containers/rhoai/odh-rhel8-operator/659803c9013347b697337263?container-tabs=dockerfile
name="managed-open-data-hub/odh-rhel8-operator"

When the container name is correct, the repository name is wrong. 
The same problem is with all OpenShift containers.

comments.author: Przemyslaw Roguski
comments.body:
This ticket should be treated as a short-term fix like @Ralph Bean mentioned already.
Generally container metadata like repository or public canonical container image name shouldn't be stored in the image layer directly, instead should be read outside of the container image layers.
 
The problem with writing a .json file to the filesystem like @Ralph Bean proposed is that during the build time, the public repository name or even the image name can be unknown yet. Adding that information during the release will change image digest sha and fail EC policy.

comments.author: Hank Donnay
comments.body:
The problem with writing a .json file to the filesystem like Ralph Bean proposed is that during the build time, the public repository name or even the image name can be unknown yet. Adding that information during the release will change image digest sha and fail EC policy.

This argument doesn't make sense to me. There are checks run on containers prior to release, right? Why couldn't that be one of them? There's nothing to do with re-writing layers, just that a container that's released to the public has its name known beforehand. All the development containers can be missing the information, so it's no up-front cost. Presumably a name for the software and a repository for it is picked before it's released. I continue to not understand why this is onerous and rejected out-of-hand as a solution, especially as having this information in the container the only way claircore (so, Clair and ACS) can support "container first" content.
That is to say, having a JSON file is great. Having it contain the information needed directly (instead of stitching together a Dockerfile or just spitting out the labels) is even better. Having that information be correct is better again.
Edit: Thinking about this more, I'm getting worked up again because recording a "canonical name" into a container manifest means it'd have to be known at build-time anyway! Changing an annotation means a new digest! Saying that claircore needs to consider the "name" of the container is like writing an analyzer to see if a binary links to old_library.so that breaks if the binary is renamed. Metadata shouldn't be affecting the results of static analysis, by definition.

comments.author: Brad Lugo
comments.body:
This issue was converted from a Bug to a Feature. I'm not sure what the implications are for doing that (particularly from a process perspective), so I wanted to quickly point out that this functionality existed previously, at least for pre-Konflux-built images. Additionally, both Clair and ACS Scanner V4 will be unable to properly index and match vulnerabilities for Container First content. Regardless, I’m happy to follow the team's process.
"Final requirements" and "Acceptance criteria" were requested from @Joseph Crosland and me, and I anticipate that whatever process we need to go through, we'll need those.
- Final requirements:  Embed each base image’s Dockerfile/Containerfile in /root/buildinfo/ where the name conforms to Dockerfile-$PRODUCT-$VERSION and, at a minimum, the following OCI Annotations 
- com.redhat.component

- name

- architecture


- Acceptance criteria: Claircore is able to report on Container First content as it could before Konflux

These final requirements are rather prescriptive to move this ticket along with minimal changes to claircore and allow current versions of Clair and ACS to operate with minimal changes (ideally, no changes at all). However, I want to provide some context about these requirements and what we might be able to do in the future:
In the rhcc scanner, i.e., the Container First scanner, we need the name-version-release information of each base image to index and match vulnerabilities properly. In claircore’s current implementation, we look for the following OCI Annotations in the embedded Dockerfiles:
- com.redhat.component

- name

- architecture
Each Dockerfile name is also used to give us a hint about the version-release string.

I also want to note that Ralph’s current proposal is problematic for us. If Konflux produces labels specifically to /root/buildinfo/labels.json, we’ll encounter a couple of possible scenarios:
-  Squash layers: If all the layers are squashed, we won’t be able to get the labels from any of the previous Dockerfiles, which would render the results from the rhcc scanner incorrect, i.e., false negatives - the worst kind of incorrect reporting from claircore’s perspective.

-  Non-squash layers: Since claircore looks through each layer, we’ll be able to determine the labels via labels.json file is added for each layer, but the last layer will contain a labels.json that has only the labels from the current build, making it difficult to debug issues in the rhcc scanner

@Ladislav Kolacek, please let me know if there's anything else for me/us to do. Looking at the Feature Refinement process, it seems like the Feature Assignee needs to put together a doc; I can contribute some information to that when it's available. I'm also happy to discuss these specifics in the Slack thread you linked above.

comments.author: Przemyslaw Roguski
comments.body:
I would propose to revisit the Final Requirements, because the requested data and especially the OCI Annotations are not good enough to allow precise container first content and security metadata detection.
Other scanning vendors use different approach and metadata to determine the container name, version and repository and solution that we need here must be universal. 
Including all Dockerfiles like it is done in the legacy build systems do not bring any value, because these Docker files are not associated in any way to the container image layers.
Included Docker files gives a high level overview to how many other base images were used before the final image has been created, but it does not give any information about the included content.
For example:
https://catalog.redhat.com/software/containers/openshift4/ose-cloud-event-proxy-rhel8/60ef3725c0dc0487102e2e88?container-tabs=dockerfile
In this image you will fine the following Dockerfiles:
rw-rw-r-. 1 root root 2919 Jan 28 03:47 Dockerfile-openshift-base-rhel8-v4.14.0-202501280211.p0.gf020942.assembly.stream.el8
rw-rw-r-. 1 root root 3511 Jan 28 04:15 Dockerfile-openshift-ose-base-v4.14.0-202501280211.p0.g03e5f40.assembly.stream.el8
rw-rw-r-. 1 root root 3716 Jan 28 05:32 Dockerfile-openshift-ose-cloud-event-proxy-rhel8-v4.14.0-202501280211.p0.g770f00b.assembly.stream.el8
rw-rw-r-. 1 root root 1839 Jun  5  2024 Dockerfile-ubi8-8.10-901.1717584420

But only the first Dockerfile describes the image, other are not related to this particular image and not to the image layers that Claircore scans. 
Mentioned problems:
- Squash layers: If all the layers are squashed, we won’t be able to get the labels from any of the previous Dockerfiles, which would render the results from the rhcc scanner incorrect, i.e., false negatives - the worst kind of incorrect reporting from claircore’s perspective.

- Non-squash layers: Since claircore looks through each layer, we’ll be able to determine the labels via labels.json file is added for each layer, but the last layer will contain a labels.json that has only the labels from the current build, making it difficult to debug issues in the rhcc scanner


are not valid, and including earlier base images Dockerfiles has nothing to do with container images layers squashing. 
 
For the precise mapping to the CSAF/VEX security metadata and container first content detection only the container name, repository, tag and optionally the architecture are needed.
For the mentioned above container image, in the Dockerfile labales you will find:
LABEL \
        name="openshift/ose-cloud-event-proxy-rhel8" \
        com.redhat.component="cloud-event-proxy-container" \

Where the name contains a wrong repository path "openshift/" instead of "openshift4/" and that's why ProdSec must maintain the  https://security.access.redhat.com/data/metrics/container-name-repos-map.json to address this gap. 
"openshift/ose-cloud-event-proxy-rhel8": 
["openshift4/cloud-event-proxy-rhel8","openshift4/ose-cloud-event-proxy-rhel8"],
The com.redhat.component OCI Annotation contains the internal NVR build name, which is not useful as long as you don't use PYXIS endpoint to verify the NVR build, which is not the case for Clair/Claircore as disconnected type scanner. I asked already earlier why you need this OCI Annotation, because the only use case where it's used is the ProdSec container name to repos mapping script as I know.
 
For the container first content scanning the /root/buildinfo/labels.json proposed by @Ralph Bean should be enough if there is included `name` or `fullname` OCI Annotation which include the full name of the component, including it's repository and tag. Like: 
`openshift4/ose-cloud-event-proxy-rhel8:v4.14.0-202501280211.p0.g770f00b.assembly.stream.el8`
or even
`registry.redhat.io/openshift4/ose-cloud-event-proxy-rhel8:v4.14.0-202501280211.p0.g770f00b.assembly.stream.el8`
Exactly the same data you will find in the Red Hat CSAF file (see: https://security.access.redhat.com/data/csaf/v2/advisories/2025/rhsa-2025_0839.json ):
"category": "product_version",
"name": "openshift4/ose-cloud-event-proxy-rhel8@sha256:daa398335f2aec22dad855bfce34f89c9613d4cb5d136f6d9d388cd505161b6f_amd64",
"product": {"name": "openshift4/ose-cloud-event-proxy-rhel8@sha256:daa398335f2aec22dad855bfce34f89c9613d4cb5d136f6d9d388cd505161b6f_amd64",

comments.body:
Including all Dockerfiles like it is done in the legacy build systems do not bring any value, because these Docker files are not associated in any way to the container image layers.

I don't 100% understand this comment, my understanding is that each image produced by the legacy build system is adding a dockerfile and ergo; if an image is based off-of RH produced images you just end up with a N Dockerfiles in the same directory. We can tie it to layers because we will see in which layer these Dockerfiles are added. (I'm not saying these other Dockerfiles are useful, just mentioning that that is my understanding of how they end up there).
But only the first Dockerfile describes the image, other are not related to this particular image and not to the image layers that Claircore scans.

They are related in as much as the eventual image we're analyzing was using them as a base layer. If you are saying that we should not care about, for example, UBI advisories in this case because prodsec data will also be listing the same vulnerabilities affecting the 
Dockerfile-openshift-base-rhel8-v4.14.0-202501280211.p0.gf020942.assembly.stream.el8 image (and every image between) then I think that makes sense, I'd just note that that is different from how the Dockerfile/legacy build system functionality is working today.
Mentioned problems:
        Squash layers: If all the layers are squashed, we won’t be able to get the labels from any of the previous Dockerfiles, which would render the results from the rhcc scanner incorrect, i.e., false negatives - the worst kind of incorrect reporting from claircore’s perspective.
        Non-squash layers: Since claircore looks through each layer, we’ll be able to determine the labels via labels.json file is added for each layer, but the last layer will contain a labels.json that has only the labels from the current build, making it difficult to debug issues in the rhcc scanner
are not valid, and including earlier base images Dockerfiles has nothing to do with container images layers squashing. 

The point was that; if we were expecting the same functionality as before (which I understand might not be the case) and every RH produced layer was adding a labels.json file to eventual image, clair would/will see those individual labels.json files in the individual layers and all except the last one would be overwritten in the final layer (if layers were squashed clair would only ever see the last one, which again, might be moot if now we only care about the last one).
The com.redhat.component OCI Annotation contains the internal NVR build name, which is not useful as long as you don't use PYXIS endpoint to verify the NVR build, which is not the case for Clair/Claircore as disconnected type scanner. I asked already earlier why you need this OCI Annotation, because the only use case where it's used is the ProdSec container name to repos mapping script as I know

In the implementation it is used to derive the "source package"'s name, I'm not sure it is strictly needed for matching as the name label and its associated repos derived from the container-name-repos-map.json are also included and would match to advisories.
 
All in all, I think everyone is a large +1 for getting rid of the container-name-repos-map.json if it is possible and getting as close as possible to the metadata in the VEX files is obviously very beneficial.

@Joseph Crosland see my answers below:
Including all Dockerfiles like it is done in the legacy build systems do not bring any value, because not all included Dockerfiles are associated in with the container image layers. In fact usually only two Dockerfiles are correct. Rest represents different data. 
 
I don't 100% understand this comment, my understanding is that each image produced by the legacy build system is adding a dockerfile and ergo; if an image is based off-of RH produced images you just end up with a N Dockerfiles in the same directory. We can tie it to layers because we will see in which layer these Dockerfiles are added. (I'm not saying these other Dockerfiles are useful, just mentioning that that is my understanding of how they end up there).

 
Let's take the example image I mentioned in my earlier comment:
https://catalog.redhat.com/software/containers/openshift4/ose-cloud-event-proxy-rhel8/60ef3725c0dc0487102e2e88?container-tabs=dockerfile
There are 4 container image layers:
                    "sha256:75401ea2a61284c039a59a40d65f9497af8d37218f3244d544f2b9a370ac0f12",
                    "sha256:639fb7d045f5ec6b207b67eaafbcd65c67314394180ed6e3bb6b9cc45a8417c7",
                    "sha256:8db9322116040597e2cd5b1529daecf0ffa93263d33d92f757c88549bf9dfff0",
                    "sha256:d349ceb2eee6a35382e8469c95c0c11908bab1c9fa23c0425c3c83c522c938a2"
And in the /root/buildinfo/ there are following Dockerfiles:
Dockerfile-openshift-base-rhel8-v4.14.0-202501280211.p0.gf020942.assembly.stream.el8
Dockerfile-openshift-ose-cloud-event-proxy-rhel8-v4.14.0-202501280211.p0.g770f00b.assembly.stream.el8
Dockerfile-openshift-ose-base-v4.14.0-202501280211.p0.g03e5f40.assembly.stream.el8
Dockerfile-ubi8-8.10-901.1717584420
These Dockerfiles do not reflect the container image layers. Using them for any layer level security validation does not bring any value.
The example container image "openshift4/ose-cloud-event-proxy-rhel8" Dockerfile is "Dockerfile-openshift-ose-cloud-event-proxy-rhel8-v4.14.0-202501280211.p0.g770f00b.assembly.stream.el8". 
This image is build based on the openshift-ose-base:v4.14.0.20250128.022007 (see parent image in brew build details: https://brewweb.engineering.redhat.com/brew/buildinfo?buildID=3484476) and it's visible in the openshift4/ose-cloud-event-proxy-rhel8 Dockerfile in line:
`FROM openshift/ose-base:v4.14.0.20250128.022007 AS bin`
For that parent image there is Dockerfile-openshift-ose-base-v4.14.0-202501280211.p0.g03e5f40.assembly.stream.el8 in the /root/buildinfo/.
That parent image is built based on the "openshift-base-rhel8:v4.14.0.20250128.022007" image (see parent image section in the brew https://brewweb.engineering.redhat.com/brew/buildinfo?buildID=3484247) which is built based on the ubi8-container-8.10-901.1717584420 (https://brewweb.engineering.redhat.com/brew/buildinfo?buildID=3484202).  
It means that the below Dockerfiles:
Dockerfile-openshift-base-rhel8-v4.14.0-202501280211.p0.gf020942.assembly.stream.el8
Dockerfile-ubi8-8.10-901.1717584420
from the above 4 are relate to the parent image build process, not the image that you scan here, which is "openshift4/ose-cloud-event-proxy-rhel8".
I hope it makes sense.
 

But only the first Dockerfile describes the image, other are not related to this particular image and not to the image layers that Claircore scans.
 
They are related in as much as the eventual image we're analyzing was using them as a base layer. If you are saying that we should not care about, for example, UBI advisories in this case because prodsec data will also be listing the same vulnerabilities affecting the 
Dockerfile-openshift-base-rhel8-v4.14.0-202501280211.p0.gf020942.assembly.stream.el8 image (and every image between) then I think that makes sense, I'd just note that that is different from how the Dockerfile/legacy build system functionality is working today.

From the non-rpm content scanning perspective the important is only the final image that is shipped to the user.
It's not important how the content was added and in which container image layer, because the final security data will be published against the final image name and repository.
That's why I proposed that for the container first content scanning the /root/buildinfo/labels.json proposed by @Ralph Bean should be enough if there is included `name` or `fullname` OCI Annotation which include the full name of the component, including it's repository and tag. Like: 
`openshift4/ose-cloud-event-proxy-rhel8:v4.14.0-202501280211.p0.g770f00b.assembly.stream.el8`
or even
`registry.redhat.io/openshift4/ose-cloud-event-proxy-rhel8:v4.14.0-202501280211.p0.g770f00b.assembly.stream.el8`
Having additional information about the product itself (as CPE id) will only improve the situation and give precise information what it is and as which product it was released.

comments.author: Jason Shepherd
comments.body:
Is there any particular version scheme enforced by Containers shipped via Konflux? I say that because when we enabled container-first scanning on RHCC initially we had to turn it off again because it assumed RPM version schematics when comparing versions. Unfortunately it was discovered some repos in the RHCC didn't use that scheme, but used things like git commit (short) hashes or similar.
Another alternative I can think of is to update the security data to use the sha256 image digest instead of a 'fixed' version. However the only way a scanner like Clair could compare that to the current image being scanned is for it to inspect the registry and compare something like the .Created label, eg:
...for both images
TIMESTAMP1=$(skopeo inspect docker://registry.example.com/myapp@sha256:digest1 | jq -r '.Created')
TIMESTAMP2=$(skopeo inspect docker://registry.example.com/myapp@sha256:digest2 | jq -r '.Created')

# Compare timestamps
if [[ "$TIMESTAMP1" > "$TIMESTAMP2" ]]; then
    echo...
This gets even more complicated by the fact that sometimes multiple update streams can ship to the same repository. In that case the 2 streams should be identifiable from each other somehow, so that a fix for one does not get incorrectly get matched to the other. I think in Konflux each stream has a unique CPE. That was NOT the case with older images from OSBS/Brew. We had to use minor versions as an indicator that multiple streams existed. Another reason why we should always include a CPE, or some other stream identifier in the 'Labels' as well. 
Stepping back from original approach taken by Clair for container-first scanning perhaps there is a better way for containers built and shipped from Konflux. What if we used the SBOM's available in the registry alongside the images instead (cosign download sbom <image-ref>). All the data we are talking about could then be added to those, and they could be used instead to compare with Security Data. This also has the added benefit of enumerating all the bundled dependencies in the image identified during the build process.
- Container name

- Version 

- Date Created

- Stream identifier (CPE is possible)

- Kind

- Arch

See also this issue for [release-time SBOMs|CLOUDWF-10908] in the registry. Unfortunately CPE is not included in release-time SBOMs. They are only available in product SBOMs, which are produced as a result of the Konflux Advisory process. I'm not sure if or where they will be shipped, I know only that they are uploaded to our internal RHTPA instead, named Atlas.

comments.author: Hank Donnay
comments.body:
Another alternative I can think of is to update the security data to use the sha256 image digest instead of a 'fixed' version. However the only way a scanner like Clair could compare that to the current image being scanned is for it to inspect the registry and compare something like the .Created label.

You hit on the reason this doesn't work: the values aren't ordered and it'd require calling registry APIs. An optimal solution would only require information in the layer. Needing to make RPCs is a last resort (painful for disconnected environments), and calling back to the registry is right out.†
What if we used the SBOMs available in the registry alongside the images instead.

Setting aside that this would be a large amount of net-new functionality in Clair, this is trivially foiled by a customer not using tooling that copies these around, or forgetting to do so, or not wanting anything that's not a container image in their registry. Requiring their use would also make Clair basically impossible to use correctly for layered products.
For example, if a customer builds an image on-top of a Red Hat image and then pushes it to their registry, all of the tooling involved would need know that linked SBOMs (no spec defined for how that relation works) need to be copied and re-linked to the resulting manifest. Hopefully they're also scoped correctly so that it's possible to tell that the SBOM does not apply to the manifest, but instead specific layers. Failing to copy all the SBOM data and metadata around correctly and keep it linked and scoped correctly would result the in Red Hat image not being indexed "correctly" if the layers were first seen without the SBOM and stay that way for the lifetime of the Clair instance.‡
So yes, Rogue is right in saying "Clair requires offline access to all metadata and everything must be added to the container image file system." We should only reconsider relaxing the latter constraint if it's not possible at all to do so. It seems to me that it's possible to provide all the needed information to the build system up-front, at the cost of at most one extra build cycle.⹋

†: Clair has no user model, and so has way of handling credentials for talking to a registry. Quay quite reasonably treats global read access as a super-user power, and Clair would require global read access. Quay.io also does not have super users.
‡: "Correctly" is in scare quotes because Clair would consider it correct: it used all the data presented to it. Also, there are ways to trigger re-indexing layers but they cannot be triggered from the HTTP API, by design. Changing things to be able to combat the case described would also mean any client would have to be extremely complex and be able to determine, by itself, that a set of layers is "actually" a Red Hat image and Clair's data does not reflect that.
⹋: If a container makes it all the way to RC and fails a release check because of missing metadata, presumably the team could just request the needed information from ProdSec, plug it into the build configuration, and trigger a new build of the exact same source code. If someone puts the information into the build configuration before the image makes it all the way through QE, it's not even an extra rebuild.

comments.author: Hank Donnay
comments.body:
Right, we need whatever information will be used in the VEX data, ideally in the exact same terms without needing an intermediary mapping step.
Any defined format should be fine, but must have:
- The same namespacing and name as the security data; it shouldn't be that the recorded name is openshift/something-operator and the name referenced in the VEX data is openshift4/advanced-cluster-something.

- Any versioning must be ordered within the namespace and name. This means it's not possible to use something like git commit SHAs, as they do not have an ordering.

comments.author: David Kaferad
comments.body:
TL;DR; Konflux currently faces a limitation in fully supporting the shipment of multiple RHEL versions for a single component due to a lack of complete functionality for Common Platform Enumerations (CPEs). This issue is actively being tracked under SDENGINE-145 and KONFLUX-6854, eliminating the need for creating new tasks.
 
Understanding CPEs:
CPEs are a standardized naming convention for software, operating systems, and hardware, crucial for security and product tracking. They are used to identify vulnerabilities, track product updates, and pinpoint broken components. ProdSec (Product Security) assigns CPEs for officially supported products with SKUs, maintaining them in their product-definitions repository. While mandatory for General Availability (GA) releases, CPEs are not required for tech-previews and should not be shared across different products to prevent incorrect patch notifications.
 
CPEs within Konflux:
ProdSec configures CPEs in Konflux, with necessary information provided in the ProdSec repository for approval. At release time, the CPE is included in the releaseNotes section of the Release Plan Admission (RPA) but should not remain in the RPA itself. Konflux enforces CPE rules through the Enterprise Contract (Conforma), ensuring that repository IDs correspond to known CPE IDs.
 
The Challenge of Multiple RHEL Versions and CPEs:
The requirement for multiple CPEs when handling different RHEL versions (e.g., RHEL 8 and RHEL 9 content) stems from the fact that a CPE combines the product short name, version, and base OS version. Although a single RPA could theoretically support multiple CPEs and product streams, this could disrupt the advisories workflow. This problem is being addressed by the SDENGINE-145 epic, which aims to enable support for multiple CPE IDs in a Konflux advisory, with implementation efforts focused on KONFLUX-6854.
Desired Outcome:
This enhancement would also benefit the push-artifacts-to-cdn pipeline, which relies on advisory tasks, ensuring consistency. The ultimate goal is to empower users to release a single update to multiple product versions or supported channels (EngIDs and CPE IDs). This is particularly relevant for RHEL products and container-based products that combine RHEL 8 and RHEL 9 images. Achieving this requires the ability to specify a CPE ID as a list within Konflux advisories and a precise mapping between the CPE (product variant) and the component.

comments.author: David Kaferad
comments.body: NOTE: There is a separate discussion currently ongoing about how to best migrate the shipping of OCP's clients / installers to Konflux. That use-case is still being investigated separately, and so far it seems it might not be depending on multiple CPEs as much. However, a more deeper dive is needed before this can be confirmed.

KFLUXSPRT-4876.description:
Request type: Feature Request
 Reason of urgency: Not urgent
Request info
Team: osci-rhel-containers
Tenant: https://konflux-ui.apps.stone-prod-p02.hjvn.p1.openshiftapps.com/ns/osci-rhel-containers-tenant
Application: rhel
Details:
Defnine product_id per components
Currently RHEL container RPA normally has a list of components per RPA and the product_id is defined under releaseNotes one per file
```    releaseNotes:
      product_id: \[70, 73, 292, 584\]
      product_name: Red Hat Enterprise Linux
      product_version: "9.4"```
But not all the components are built for 4 arches, so we split the RPA by arches support combination, like all arches in one RPA, 3 arches, 2 arches ... etc

This bright some side effects, like
• additional RPA, RP to manage
• think we can not create subfolder for RPA, so the number of RPAs for the tenants growing fast
• unnecessary release pipeline will be triggered as we have multiple RPAs per application.
If the product id can be override on components level, like default value is defined under releaseNotes, then can be 3 or 2 arches only for some of the components. It will help to reduce the number of RPA/RP created.

Support for multiple product_id is needed to support future RHEL rpm releases, similarly like it's supported today in the Errata Tool. There is no high pressure to ave it right now, as for now even RHEL 10 rpm Konflux builds won't be released through Konlfux advisory pipeline but the legacy Errata Tool pipeline will be used. 
The multiple CPE support is something that is more important now, because this will allow existing Konflux user to simplify their current workflow and instead of releasing RHEL8 amd RHEL9 based images separately (because there are different CPEs) they will be able to release them in one advisory.
Even if this is a user experience improvement, it's not critical though.

SDENGINE-145.description:
Title / Epic Summary
Support for multiple CPEs in Konflux Advisory OR support for multiple CPEs and RPM-based content in Konflux Advisory, based on CY25Q2 and CY25Q3 external factors (Konflux team will say which it is when the time comes).
Outcome
Desired outcome: SDEngine processes Konflux Advisories based on a new (not yet existing as of CY25Q1) schema that includes multiple CPEs or multiple CPEs and RPMs. This is then used similarly to errata tool advisories to generate content for CVE pages, CSAF, VEX, OVAL.
Acceptance Criteria
- SDEngine consumes konflux advisories from https://gitlab.cee.redhat.com/releng/advisories/-/blob/main/data/advisories .

- The advisories are in a format described by a specification, such as https://gitlab.cee.redhat.com/releng/advisories/-/blob/main/schema/advisory.json?ref_type=heads

- The specification is different from the specification already used in production as of CY25Q1 and includes the new features (multiple CPEs, RPMs).

- Konflux and SDEngine teams agree on that specificaiton and agree on a specific date and time when both teams/systems switch from the old format to the new format.

- The change happens successfully, SDEngine processes the advisories (see point 1) correctly.

Details
Are there any specifications or details relevant to this request?
TBD, but also see below
Relevant Stakeholders
On Konflux side:
@Johnny Bieren 
@Przemyslaw Roguski 
On SDEngine side:
@Chuntao Han (Hank)
@Jakub Svoboda 
Impact Statement
What is the impact of this request? For example: How many users are impacted? How much money is saved? What are the consequences if we don't do this?
Understanding of the Impact Statement requires understanding of the reason Konflux and SDEngine projects exist. Such understanding then means the impact is clear.
So to state the obvious: This is critical and enables Red Hat's continued stream of information to CVE Pages, CSAF, VEX, OVAL. It impacts all Red Hat and most customers, many non-customers, RH's reputation. Probably saves untold amount of money in fines. I'm not able to properly list the consequences of not doing this.
Target Start Date
What is the desired start of the Epic? Are there any due dates or delivery expectations? If so please explain.
Start probably CY25Q2 or CY25Q3 based on input from Konflux team.
SDEngine can't do anything without Konflux team first creating a new version of the advisory spec (at least draft). That might change based on external factors that put a pressure on Konflux directly (not on SDEngine directly).
Possible preparation on SDEngine side already done (see comments, there are links to documents and drawings; two SDEngine engineers are already reasonably familiar with the code structure to be able to start the implementation when the time comes).
(the above written on 2025-03-12 based on the meeting "Resolve questions on multiple cpe id support" with Rogue, Yuli, Hank, Jakub, Marek)

Original Description as written by John Bieren:
(Leaving the original description without edits, because it captures the viewpoint of the Konflux team, which is different enough that I would miss important nuances.)
 
Title / Epic Summary
Support multiple cpe id in konflux advisory.
Outcome
In some cases users want to release one update to many product versions or supported channels, which is represented by many EngIDs and sometimes many CPE ids. This is a typical use case in RHEL products. In the container based products many times users want to mix RHEL8 based images with RHEL9 based images, which requires associations with more than one CPE id.
Hence we need to specify a CPE id as a list in the Konflux advisories.
For CPE id we need precise mapping between CPE (product variant) and component.
 
Acceptance Criteria
SDEngine can consume new Konflux advisory schema and produce correct content in the security metadata (CVE pages and CSAF/VEX files).
This include mapping between CPE id to product and component.
 
Relevant Stakeholders
On Konflux side:
@Johnny Bieren 
@Przemyslaw Roguski 
Impact Statement
Once Konflux is used to release RPM content, then this functionality will be critical. Which is Q2/2025 as I understand.
For the container container this is nice to have functionality, but is not critical.
 
Target Start Date
It would be good to have this functionality ready to use in at the beginning of Q2/2025 (there is no hard target GA date)

comments.author: Tomas Popela
comments.body:
@Przemyslaw Roguski after talking to @Owen Taylor and @Ralph Bean we went with excluding the rpm_repos.ids_known checks (https://gitlab.cee.redhat.com/releng/konflux-release-data/-/merge_requests/4396).
Why the Firefox and Thunderbird Flatpaks cannot be built and shipped in a normal way?

They can't because of how Flatpak works. Quoting https://developers.redhat.com/blog/2020/08/12/introducing-the-red-hat-flatpak-runtime-for-desktop-containers#flatpak_runtimes:
```
Creating an application involves creating an application image that, at runtime, will be mounted at /app. The application image goes along with the runtime image, which is mounted at /usr. There are various ways to create these images. For example, Fedora creates Flatpaks out of Red Hat Package Managers (RPMs). RPMs are rebuilt and installed into a container image within Fedora's container build system. 
```
We can't use the regular Firefox or Thunderbird packages as they are built with the regular /usr prefix. Prior to RHEL 10 we've been using Modularity to do builds with /app prefix and in RHEL 10 where Modularity isn't presented we're using a special brew target rhel-10-flatpak-app-build (created in https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHELBLD-15176#icft=RHELBLD-15176
) that has a special flatpak-rpm-macros package installed that changes the prefix to /app (see https://gitlab.com/redhat/centos-stream/rpms/flatpak-rpm-macros/-/blob/c10s/macros.flatpak.in?ref_type=heads#L3). This is then used to create the applications Flatpaks - https://gitlab.com/redhat/rhel/containers/firefox/-/blob/rhel-10.0/flatpak-app-build.repo?ref_type=heads.
As I can see this is you last firefox:flatpak errata: https://errata.devel.redhat.com/advisory/144415
And it was released as a part of the Hidden product variant, but from the public perspective there are real Red Hat rpm packages there: https://access.redhat.com/errata/RHBA-2025:0933

This is the Flatpak module that contains the special build of Firefox with /app prefix. These modules are not shipped to any customers (hence Hidden repository), but are used to create the Flatpak container which is shipped to customers - https://errata.devel.redhat.com/package/show/firefox-flatpak-container / https://pkgs.devel.redhat.com/cgit/containers/firefox/tree/container.yaml?h=rhel-9.5.0
the Firefox and Thunderbird Flatpaks components will be built and released in a standard way to the official repositories (even if CDN repo is not accessible)

PSDEVOPS-4341.description:
Initially when we designed konflux fetching we wanted to use a 'comparable version' for container images. No such thing existed, so we decided to generate an integer version based on the build end date.
Now that we are returning PURLs in NewCLI, it's more useful to use the image digest as the version. It seems that can be found in the current attestations of the image, around about:
$ cosign download attestation registry.redhat.io/costmanagement/costmanagement-metrics-rhel9-operator:latest | jq -r .payload | base64 -d | jq '.predicate.buildConfig.tasks[].invocation.parameters.IMAGE_DIGEST'

...
"sha256:aaff1e2e5ceae6e1ba91c32e60e5260883a8d4842895ed367d273afab303d1f2"
...
As long as there is only a single stream of images in a repository we should be able to compare image digests using the repository metadata:
# Get timestamps for both images
TIMESTAMP1=$(skopeo inspect docker://registry.example.com/myapp@sha256:digest1 | jq -r '.Created')
TIMESTAMP2=$(skopeo inspect docker://registry.example.com/myapp@sha256:digest2 | jq -r '.Created')

# Compare timestamps
if [[ "$TIMESTAMP1" > "$TIMESTAMP2" ]]; then
    echo "digest1 is newer"
else
    echo "digest2 is newer"
fi

comments.author: Brad Lugo
comments.body:
Assigning this to myself since I’ve been looking through/helping out with the Claircore code and have been following the various threads of discussion. Here’s the current state of things:
The Konflux team will add a patch to add content sets back into images

This work was completed, tracked via KONFLUX-6200. Verification/example:
❯ docker run --platform linux/amd64 --rm --user root -it registry.redhat.io/rhel9/nginx-124@sha256:4dd6bce207c829ee5e66b8e02218ce8d315345893611b1241ead6cb0f36fa89e cat /root/buildinfo/content_manifests/content-sets.json
{
  "metadata": {
    "icm_version": 1,
    "icm_spec": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/containerbuildsystem/atomic-reactor/master/atomic_reactor/schemas/content_manifest.json",
    "image_layer_index": 0
  },
  "from_dnf_hint": true,
  "content_sets": [
    "rhel-9-for-aarch64-appstream-rpms",
    "rhel-9-for-aarch64-appstream-source-rpms",
    "rhel-9-for-aarch64-baseos-rpms",
    "rhel-9-for-aarch64-baseos-source-rpms",
    "rhel-9-for-ppc64le-appstream-rpms",
    "rhel-9-for-ppc64le-appstream-source-rpms",
    "rhel-9-for-ppc64le-baseos-rpms",
    "rhel-9-for-ppc64le-baseos-source-rpms",
    "rhel-9-for-s390x-appstream-rpms",
    "rhel-9-for-s390x-appstream-source-rpms",
    "rhel-9-for-s390x-baseos-rpms",
    "rhel-9-for-s390x-baseos-source-rpms",
    "rhel-9-for-x86_64-appstream-rpms",
    "rhel-9-for-x86_64-appstream-source-rpms",
    "rhel-9-for-x86_64-baseos-rpms",
    "rhel-9-for-x86_64-baseos-source-rpms"
  ]
}
Both ACS and Clair teams will update Claircore to read the relevant information out of the dnf database, which will be present in all Konflux-build images (and is present in all current Konflux-built images, too)

This work is currently in progress and tracked via CLAIRDEV-41. I want to flag that during this work, we discovered that UBI images do not preserve dnf database files in the final layer. As of now, we’re not sure if any other images are affected, but we spot-checked a few dozen images built on top of UBI, and they seem to have all the necessary dnf files. For more information and progress regarding that bug, see https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/ENGCMP-5332#icft=ENGCMP-5332
.

Konflux builds images without these files, so these scanners are unable to accurately match found RPMs to vulnerabilities, and they are unable to identify the name+version of the related Red Hat image to match against "container-first" content.

This root cause requires a different fix from the other two, so I suppose the overall solution for this Jira issue is threefold. The solution to this problem will be the outcome of KONFLUX-6210. Currently, we're trying to figure out the best approach for adding the necessary information for the rhcc scanner (AKA Container first scanning) and how we can add this information to the container image during build time without changing the digest of the container image. Please see KONFLUX-6210 for further analysis/discussion and progress.

comments.author: Patrick Ladd
comments.body:
Priority bump on this - my customer CIBC bank has noted a discrepancy on container health image on two fairly similar python images:
- "D" for newer image https://catalog.redhat.com/software/containers/ubi9/python-312/657b08d023df896ebfacf402?image=677e7b2ae58b5a1ae55da231&container-tabs=security

- "A" for slightly older image https://catalog.redhat.com/software/containers/ubi9/python-312/657b08d023df896ebfacf402?image=674e0d453f62d351ea49476a&container-tabs=security

CIBC primarily relies on our CHI grade for using images, but a secondary scan with Aqua noted vulnerabilities in the "A" grade image and raised a question.
 
My understanding from discussion in slack thread on #forum-metadata-guild is that the manifest file needed to grade the older image is missing.  However, this results in the container being graded as "A" rather than "Unknown" or "F".  This is a HUGE PROBLEM - anyone that visits that second image in the catalog and assumes that it's good to deploy is exposed to any number of unknown CVEs with no warning.  All of the effort to promote the use of our container health index is destroyed by this problem.
Discussion with @Subhro Kar from prod-sec team led me to this Jira.  I expect that we urgently implement some sort of fix to stop inaccurately reporting unscannable images as "A" grades ASAP.  Ideally for longer term, properly scanning older images is preferable.  There is major impact to Red Hat's security reputation and our brand as long as we continue default to reporting images that are not properly scanned as "A" CHI grade.  Imagine a major security breach that results from a customer relying on our "A" grade on a container image with critical vulnerabilities in it.
I can hold off on reporting this situation back to my customer for a bit longer, but the process of explaining the situation as it exists today is seriously embarrassing.

ROX-27482.description:
USER PROBLEM
What is the user experiencing as a result of the bug? Include steps to reproduce.
- Users will find 0 vulnerabilities related to rpms and container-first data for official Red Hat images.

CONDITIONS
What conditions need to exist for a user to be affected? Is it everyone? Is it only those with a specific integration? Is it specific to someone with particular database content? etc.
- Any image built via Konflux is affected by this.

ROOT CAUSE
What is the root cause of the bug?
- Both StackRox Scanner (Scanner v2) and Scanner V4 (built over Claircore) require "content sets" inside of /root/buildinfo/content_manifests/ as well as Dockerfile images inside of /root/buildinfo/ to accurately identify RPM and non-RPM content in official Red Hat images and match them to the appropriate set of vulnerabilities.

- Konflux builds images without these files, so these scanners are unable to accurately match found RPMs to vulnerabilities, and they are unable to identify the name+version of the related Red Hat image to match against "container-first" content.

FIX
How was the bug fixed (this is more important if a workaround was implemented rather than an actual fix)?
- The solution is twofold:
- The Konflux team will add a patch to add content sets back into images
- This requires all Konflux users to update their pipelines to use the latest Konflux version. This also only aids future builds, and past Konflux-built images will still have inaccurate scan results.


- Both ACS and Clair teams will update Claircore to read the relevant information out of the dnf database, which will be present in all Konflux-build images (and is present in all current Konflux-built images, too)
- This database existed pre-Konflux, but did not provide the accurate information we require (though we acknowledge the original content sets also lead to some inaccuracies). Konflux-provided dnf databases offer more accurate data, which will only improve our scan results.



 
TODO: We only discussed content sets and did not touch upon the missing Dockerfiles, which both ACS and Clair read to identify the relevant name+version of the official Red Hat container.
 
Please DO NOT link a customer case directly to this ticket

RELDEL-8146.description:
STF has a plethora of open reviews, one per containerfile, to add CPE text to each container. Presumably, this is because CPE is a field that Conforma complains about when it is missing.
Note that this field is controlled by Product Security: https://gitlab.cee.redhat.com/releng/konflux-release-data/-/blob/main/prodsec/openstack.yaml?ref_type=heads#L3
Here is an example of Conforma failures (from OSP13, but applies to STF as well):
› [Warning] labels.required_labels
  ImageRef: quay.io/redhat-user-workloads/openstack-tenant/openstack-13/openstack-zaqar@sha256:8c7ad647a4b712b5d32c40b28873b8f48fc0fff90a2793f069711f564fae99da
  Reason: The required "cpe" label is missing. Label description: The CPE (Common Platform Enumeration) identifier for the
  product, e.g., cpe:/a:redhat:openshift_gitops:1.16::el8. This label is required for on-prem product releases.
  Term: cpe
  Title: Required labels
  Description: Check the image for the presence of labels that are required. Use the rule data `required_labels` key to set the
  list of labels to check, or the `fbc_required_labels` key for fbc images.
  Solution: Update the image build process to set the required labels.

› [Warning] labels.required_labels
  ImageRef: quay.io/redhat-user-workloads/openstack-tenant/openstack-13/openstack-zaqar@sha256:8c7ad647a4b712b5d32c40b28873b8f48fc0fff90a2793f069711f564fae99da
  Reason: The required "org.opencontainers.image.created" label is missing. Label description: The creation timestamp of the
  image. This label must always be set by the Konflux build task for on-prem product releases. The policy must also support
  reproducible builds by allowing users to override the timestamp using the SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH environment variable.
  Term: org.opencontainers.image.created
  Title: Required labels
  Description: Check the image for the presence of labels that are required. Use the rule data `required_labels` key to set the
  list of labels to check, or the `fbc_required_labels` key for fbc images.
  Solution: Update the image build process to set the required labels.
While I do not believe these should be the problem of the user to set (if the build system requires the field and it knows the appropriate values, which it does, it should set them), I do think we can add these in the RPAs rather than to each Containerfile individually.

This appears incorrect because the packages already contain a fix for the flagged vulnerability. (In this case, CVE-2023-44487.) However, because the container name mapping points to two different package names (in these cases, openshift/proj and openshift/proj-rhel9), both are associated with the container. When the cvemap.xml file is parsed, the names are treated independently. This results in two vulnerabilities with version ranges that have an infinitely early lower bound. As an example:
- Container's "name" label: "openshift/foo"

- container-name-repos-map.json entry: ["openshift/foo", "openshift/foo-rhel9"]

- relevant cvemap.xml packages: openshift/foo:v1.0, openshift/foo-rhel9:v1.1

Two vulnerabilities will be produced, one for each cvemap.xml package. However, because the names are different, they will both produce a range with a lower bound of zero, and thus both match. This lower bound behavior is desired: consider a CVE in openshift/foo:v0.9 that has since gone out of support.

This is the same root issue as CLAIRDEV-45, only reproduced in the domain of containers instead of rpms. As long as Red Hat release artifacts don't have enough information to uniquely identify them in the same terms that are used in the security data, this phantom problem will be endemic.

comments.author: Hank Donnay
comments.body:
it'd be rad if you could provide a brief write-up here that we could point to whenever someone suggests we use this metadata or asks why we can't.

Conceptually, using metadata of a manifest or layer (primarily the tag) breaks the content-addressable invariant that's a cornerstone of how we (try) to minimize work. As a thought experiment, consider what happens when registry.redhat.io/rhel9/nginx-124:9.5-1730563934 is submitted after example.com/registry-mirror/rhel9/nginx-124:9.5-1730563934. If we considered the tag, it'd always be "first write wins." We'd also need to rely on clients to faithfully report the metadata to get "correct" results.
We could maybe mitigate this by also ingesting all the related config JSON, but that
- would be net-new functionality

- opt-in (to retain API backward compatibility)

- would require some standard "canonical name" attribute

It would be much simpler to have the build system record the "canonical name" in a layer when known and have the release pipeline enforce its presence. This would allow KONFLUX tenants the flexibility to produce nonpublic/development images and ensure that this bit of information is not separable from the container image when published.

comments.author: Hank Donnay
comments.body:
Can you explain why do you need com.redhat.component?

Looking at the claircore source as of d8601139e24e41749136dc7510ae19f2264896f7, if interested in playing along at home.
The "container first" logic (which we call rhcc) is located in rhel/rhcc/scanner.go.
The Dockerfile handling is done in findLabels.
The first file matching the glob root/buildinfo/Dockerfile-* is examined and the part of the filename after the - and the evaluated labels are returned.
The filename fragment is parsed as an NVR, and the "VR" section is assumed to be partially orderable.
The three Dockerfile labels checked for are:
- com.redhat.component

- name

- architecture

The last is used to inform the architecture of reported claircore Packages.
The name is used as a key to look up in a mapping file for container names,
and the com.redhat.component is recorded as a "source" Package for all the {{Package}}s produced by the lookup step.
This is logic from the initial contribution from Jason Shepherd.
Guessing from the outside, this allows for a container-first product's "name" to change over time and use the "component" as a backstop?

KONFLUX-15646.description:
Investigate whether image metadata (specifically labels.json) can be shipped as an OCI referrer artifact linked to the image, rather than baked into the image layers. This would allow in-place correction of metadata like the name field without requiring image rebuilds.
Context
KFLUXSPRT-8325 revealed that labels.json in some OpenShift images had incorrect name fields (e.g. openshift/image instead of openshift4/image), breaking Clair's VEX matching and causing ~5% false positive rate in vulnerability scanning across OCP 4.22.7 (80/191 core images affected). Since labels.json is baked into the image, already-shipped images cannot be corrected without a full rebuild and new release.
Proposal
dmesser (Daniel Messer) proposed using OCI referrers to attach labels.json as a separate artifact in the same registry repo, linked to the image. This would allow in-place metadata correction without image rebuilds, use the same credentials and access pathways as the image itself, and provide resilience to accidental or malicious changes via OCI referrer linking.
Questions to answer
- Can Clair/Claircore consume labels.json from an OCI referrer artifact instead of image layers?

- What changes would oc-mirror and other tooling need to support this?

- How do we handle alignment between layer content and external metadata artifacts?

- How does this relate to the existing discussion in CLAIRDEV-251 (reading labels from image config vs labels.json)?

References
- KFLUXSPRT-8325 - Original support ticket

- KONFLUX-6210 - Container-first vulnerability reporting (parent feature)

- RELEASE-1855 - Remove enforceContainerFirstSecurityLabels

- CLAIRDEV-251 - Read image labels from image config, not labels.json

This issue was created with the assistance of Claude Code.

KONFLUX-14738.summary: Enable container-first security labels for RHOAI RPAs (v2.25)

comments.author: Ryan Hartman
comments.body: Reached out in Slack

comments.author: Akshay Ghodake
comments.body:
Hi @Ryan Hartman ,
I have looked into what's needed to enable enforcement for the v2.25 RPAs. A couple of questions before we proceed:# The enforce-cpe-label check requires a releaseNotes.cpe value to be defined in the ReleasePlan data. RHOAI currently doesn't set this field, and the check-labels task will hard-fail if it's missing -- regardless of whether individual images have the cpe label or not. Do you know what the correct CPE value should be for RHOAI v2.25 (e.g., cpe:/a:redhat:openshift_ai:2.25), and where it should be defined -- in the ReleasePlan or somewhere else?
- v2.25 has 66 components. Before flipping enforcement on, we need to audit that all Dockerfiles have the correct name label matching their target registry path (e.g., LABEL name="rhoai/odh-dashboard-rhel9"). Is there an existing report or tooling that shows which images are currently non-compliant, or should we run that audit ourselves?

- For the name label, the check-labels task can derive the expected value from either the component's canonicalName field or the first repository URL. Are there any components where the canonicalName diverges from the repo path that we should be aware of?

Once we have the CPE value sorted and confirm the name labels are correct across all 66 components, the actual RPA change is straightforward -- just removing the enforceContainerFirstSecurityLabels: false line from both rhoai-onprem-v2-25-components-prod.yaml and rhoai-onprem-v2-25-components-stage.yaml.

comments.author: Ryan Hartman
comments.body:
@Akshay Ghodake Hello! So in konflux-release-data, the cpe is derived and automatically injected into your RPA. It’s defined with this template: https://gitlab.cee.redhat.com/releng/konflux-release-data/-/blob/main/prodsec/rhoai.yaml?ref_type=heads , and the values are gathered from the rpa you’re releasing with. So you need to make sure your containers have the “cpe” label in them that match that: https://konflux.pages.redhat.com/docs/users/releasing/container-first-scanning-vex.html for more info.

As for a report, if you look at the most recent release for any of your versions, the check-labels check is still running, it’s just not failing your release. So you should see warnings and be able to look at the logs to see which containers are failing

comments.author: Akshay Ghodake
comments.body:
Hi @Ryan Hartman,
I have raised a MR to remove enforceContainerFirstSecurityLabels: false from both v2.25 RPAs (stage and prod):
https://gitlab.cee.redhat.com/releng/konflux-release-data/-/merge_requests/21898
This will enable name and cpe label enforcement for RHOAI v2.25 releases, bringing it in line with v2.13-v2.21 which already have enforcement enabled.
Could you please review the MR? Before merging, we should confirm from a recent v2.25 release's check-labels task logs that no images are currently failing. If any are non-compliant, we'll need to fix their Dockerfile labels first.

comments.author: Ryan Hartman
comments.body: The MR looks good to me, approved, but i’ll let you merge it when you’re ready, but I encourage you to do it asap, if you do release an image not configured properly ACS may come knocking to have you replace it

comments.author: Justin Spencer
comments.body:
The relevant code is in the "KonfluxAdvisory" class's "update_or_create_raw()" method in the models.py file:
variant, _ = KonfluxVariant.objects.update_or_create(
    cpe=spec["cpe"],
    defaults={
        "name": spec["product_name"],
        "product_version": spec["product_version"],
        "product_stream": spec["product_stream"],
    },
)

advisory["variant"] = variant
We don't use the product_id field directly. But if multiple products will be fixed on a single advisory (and if each has a different name or stream or whatever), we'll need to iterate over the list of names / versions / streams, and create a KonfluxVariant for each.
This will also require a ManyToManyField / mapping between the KonfluxAdvisory and each KonfluxVariant it fixes, or (better solution) a ForeignKey from the KonfluxContainer to its parent KonfluxVariant.
Then we'll also need to update the CSAF-generating logic for Konflux advisories. Today we assume that one KonfluxAdvisory always refers to / fixes exactly one product, because data model requirements were not very clear when we started). You should be able to copy the same logic from the CSAF-generating logic for Errata Tool advisories, and just change "ErratumBuild" to say "KonfluxContainer" instead.
It's probably worth reviewing (and maybe refactoring, sorry) all the related code as well, since there are lots of TODOs still and the code only supports containers (not RPMs or RPM modules).
@Martin Prpic @Przemyslaw Roguski FYI, please help to coordinate this and any future Konflux changes with @Stanislav Kontar or @Yuguang Wang going forward.

The `product_id` field in the Konflux advisories is tied to the Engineering ID (EngID) which was never used by ProdSec.
EndID are used by subscription manager and later sales and marketing to define SKUs.
Having multiple product_id in the Konlfux advisories shouldn't impact SDEngine and security data (CSAF files) production at all.
In the future if there will be an intention to support many product versions in one advisory, it will be more related to the support of many CPEs in one advisory, which is tracked in separate issue:
https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/SECDATA-878

SECDATA-891.description:
Title / Epic Summary
Support multiple product_id in konflux advisory.
Please confirm if Engineering Product ID (EngID) is used in SDEngine (based on our research it's not used).
Outcome
In some cases users want to release one update to many product versions or supported channels, which is represented by many EngIDs. This is a typical use case in RHEL products. Hence we need to specify the Product ID (EngID) as a list in the Konflux advisories.
Acceptance Criteria
SDEngine can consume new Konflux advisory schema and produce correct content in the security metadata (CVE pages and CSAF/VEX files).
 
Relevant Stakeholders
On Konflux side:
@Johnny Bieren 
@Przemyslaw Roguski 
Impact Statement
Once Konflux is used to release RPM content, then this functionality will be critical. Which is Q2/2025 as I understand.
 
Target Start Date
It would be good to have this functionality ready to use in at the beginning of Q2/2025 (there is no hard target GA date)

IMPORTANT NOTE: This epic only affects products that publish customer-facing errata at https://access.redhat.com/errata
Goal: Store and display product advisory information for those advisories published by RHTAP.
Acceptance Criteria:
- When a new advisory is published by RHTAP, that data
- is consumed and stored by Unified Downloads

- is available publicly to customers at a.rh.c/errata/<type&ID>

- is included in the errata search feed for indexing on Customer Portal Errata search at a.rh.c/errata-search


- When an update to an advisory is published, the updated data is reflected in the Unified Downloads data store and all downstream feeds and displays

- When an advisory is removed (deleted OR determined that it should no longer be viewable by customers), the advisory should be removed from the Unified Downloads data store and no longer viewable by customer (note: it will still be indexed until it is manually removed due to the current integration; future improvements to this UD->Search integration will negate this, but that is many months away)

Technical Notes
- We will work with the RHTAP team to get the correct integration contracts in place

- This will likely be the first set of advisories that flow into the new data store, so we will likely need the UI to be flexible in where it pulls advisories from. i.e. look in one data store first, and if it is not found, look in the second data store, and if still not found, give a 404.

- RHTAP documentation on this feature - https://docs.google.com/document/d/18jfEH3X377A7G6LN9qVE16CH07Wfkqs7wrjSefChiOs/edit?usp=sharing

- Related: ProdSec epic to do similar things - https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/SECDATA-280

comments.author: Vaclav Tunka
comments.body:
Hi Sinbad & PgM team,
First couple of facts - as Kaustubh already did correct you, we didn’t breach the milestone again, but we shipped yesterday despite rel-eng / Konflux infra instability we have been battling with for the last couple of weeks and we made sure to align with OCP 4.19. We used to be able to release our product in 1 or days in our “legacy pipeline” before migrating to Konflux. I still yet have to see the benefit from this effort that totally broke our release predictability.
I have a couple of points for the program management group around the value add I’d expect from this function, feel free to connect with me in person after I am back from PTO in the Brno office in two weeks and I am happy to elaborate more.
Let me just recap couple of general premises and assumptions I expect as internal customer from program management and from teams supporting us as we deliver to actual real customers and partners in concert bringing revenue for the business we’re in and for our stakeholders:
- PgMs talk to each other and the various teams from the same Konflux organization

- If the Konflux org established support channels in slack where we had a blocker open for every other day in the past few weeks I’d expect program management to be at least aware if not proactive about those and reporting back on this high level jira.

- Konflux team decided to align legacy pipeline deprecation with this ticket originally focused on container onboarding (we did this months ago), I don’t consider this a good practice as it leads to shadow tracking providing false signals to Sr. Leadership. This Jira should have been closed months ago if konflux teams did tie it with legacy pipeline retirement.

- You are forcing internal customers to do all the admin for you - which cluster this is on, what’s the status etc. Instead of chasing this for us as internal customer. Where’s the value add I ask?

- I’d expect Konflux team would be asking us on program level what are the impediments they can help us get out of the way, not to ping us every day creating pressure on things you should be aware of already - see above.

I honestly put this here just for learning purposes as I thought this might be useful for more teams. I thought this is 101 I don’t need to be so explicit about.

Vaclav

comments.author: Shay Vatarescu
comments.body:
Hi @Vaclav Tunka your latest comment is inappropriate and patronizing.
We understand the frustration one might have from the process of onboarding, to a system that is not perfect and is experiencing some hiccups often. Please remember that Konflux is new system, and is being massively onboarded by dozens of teams (126 teams to be exact).
The migration team, with the amazing help from the PgM team, are tracking all of those 126 teams in 228 different trackers, and not only yours. There are more than 2600 GA image repos that are being migrated to Konflux by the different teams, from teams with a handful of images to teams with a few hundreds images.
So, please forgive us for not being able to put all of our attention on your team.
We highly appreciate all of the hard work and efforts your team have put onboarding Konflux, and would highly appreciate constructive feedback to be delivered to the Konflux program in a meaningful way, and not by stating irrelevant patronizing facts.
You are more than welcome to collect the meaningful constructive feedback your team has on the migration process to Konflux in a google doc and share it with the migration team, so we could share it with the relevant teams in Konflux and try to improve, just like many other teams the finished their migration to Konflux have done.
A clarification regarding the message coming from Sinbad, that have triggered you: the target end date, provided by you or your team, was set to June 17th. Since this date has passed yesterday, the message regarding the target date being breached was sent. This wasn't done in any way to put more pressure or frustration, but just to verify that you have not forgotten updating the tracker, as it happened with other teams in the past. Moreover, it was an opportunity to update the target date in case some issues prevented your team from finishing the migration on time.
Please reach out to me in case you're willing to share any more feedback or share the google doc with feedback from your team.

comments.author: Vaclav Tunka
comments.body:
Hi Shay,
thank you for your comment. We have been partnering with Jeff and team since last fall exactly around lessons learned from the onboarding we have been doing based on a doc we shared, last year we had Konflux architect joining our meetings - (thanks Ralph, Andrew and others!) and we have been working with all of those people collaboratively and passing feedback around - this was not the point of my comment though, point of my comment was exclusively about how we track this and the support PgM team offers here. We shared extensive lessons learned doc that led to performance improvements and architecture / design improvements, I realize Konflux is a new system that takes time to mature (it's based on Tekton/Pipelines that originally branched from our project), that's all good and we have been doing exactly what you talk about already and have been doing it for quite some time. Also you're coming from engineering org if I recall, my comment was around how the PgM team works here to support us. Again, we have finished migration of our containers long time ago as you can see in this ticket. We were keeping this ticket open only bacause konflux team decided to base enabling / disabling of legacy pipelines to this ticket, I don't think that's a good practice. We had to make sure we have 2 last minor versions of software released via konflux so we can do that and we can support our customers with z-stream / CVE fixes / urgent fixes. This was the business reason and now finally we're exclusively in konflux for all our supported streams, so thanks for the partnership.
Back to tracking things / program management angle. This is not a single instance this has been a repeated pattern and for example we don't have a PgM for our own product offering so this falls on Engineering to coordinate and do extra work - you can see all the relevant comments have been mentioned here historically about our reliance on legacy workflow etc. Konflux as a group (realize it's a lot of teams including the former RCM / SP teams doing the rel-eng work) has a support workflow in slack that y'all decided on and we as internal customers had to accept this.  How so one part of the group is not aware there's a ticket open every other day? I'd expect there's some sort of automated analysis and tagging of the support issues - you know this is coming from a specific team and this automation could also update Jira for example. So let's please get back on track of my comments on how can we improve things on tracking side and I think this is for the PgM team to own, but I am happy also to have a conversation with Konflux eng as well.
Vaclav
PS: Red Hat has a finite number of products and I doubt we have so many GA offerings, you can of course go to different level of granularity per tracking and that's a conversation we should be having - is this too much, good number of trackers etc.? How can we automate things, how can we make the support workflow easier, etc. 228 trackers seem way to much for number of products Red Hat ships in total but that's an OT conversation.

Konflux Migration Team

comments.author: Przemyslaw Roguski
comments.body:
Support multiple CPEs requires a precise mapping between the product based version (RHEL9 or RHEL8 based) to the component.
Such mapping in the legacy Errata Tool is done based on the Product Version to Build mapping.
For example:
RPM advisory (most common use case for multiple CPEs): https://errata.devel.redhat.com/advisory/145607
Container advisory (rare, but possible): https://errata.devel.redhat.com/advisory/145417
 
It means that in the RPA we need somehow map the product based to the associated components.
Today the RHEL based information is handled via custom `rhel_target` field in the annotations metadata, like:
https://gitlab.cee.redhat.com/releng/konflux-release-data/-/tree/main/config/stone-prd-rh01.pg1f.p1/product/ReleasePlanAdmission/3scale-prod?ref_type=heads
If we want to allow user to use one RPA instead of two, then we have to extend the RPA spec to have:
components:
    - name:
    repository:
    rhel_target: (optional field)
 
Once it's set, then user can use one RPA for RHEL8 and RHEL9 builds with multiple CPEs.
@Ralph Bean just FYI
